name: Vega machine

card.summary: An electrodermal screening device that measures skin conductance at a probe point while the patient holds test vials, used by some practitioners to identify food and environmental sensitivities that people link to skin and body concerns.
card.aka: Vega test; Vegatest; electrodermal screening; EAV
card.note: Medical and allergy bodies have stated the method lacks an established scientific basis.

quick.overview:
The Vega machine is a skin-conductance device used in electrodermal testing. A practitioner attaches an electrode to the patient, presses a probe to a skin point and reads a meter while the patient holds glass vials of substances such as foods. Practitioners interpret the readings as signs of sensitivity or intolerance and suggest dietary changes.

In appearance communities it is mentioned as a way of identifying foods or products believed to cause skin problems such as breakouts or inflammation. Medical bodies including the Australian College of Allergy have stated that Vega testing has no established scientific basis, and a double-blind study found electrodermal testing could not distinguish atopic from non-atopic participants.
quick.how: Sessions are offered by complementary and naturopathic practitioners. The patient holds an electrode while the practitioner touches a probe to a point on the hand or foot and notes the meter reading as different substance vials are introduced. The result is typically followed by a suggestion to remove certain foods or substances.
quick.risks: No physical harm comes from the measurement itself. The documented concern, stated by the Australian College of Allergy, is that Vega testing may lead to inappropriate treatment and expense, such as unnecessary dietary restriction in place of conventional allergy evaluation.

lead: The Vega machine, also called the Vegatest or Vega II, is an electrodermal testing device: electronics that measure skin conductance through a probe pressed against the skin.[1] In a typical session the patient holds glass tubes containing different substances while the practitioner reads the device's gauge and uses the readings to diagnose sensitivities such as dairy or gluten intolerance.[1]

People interested in improving their skin or general appearance sometimes use such sessions to look for foods or products believed to trigger breakouts or inflammation, and then adjust their diet based on the result. Practitioners and proponents regard the readings as informative about the body's reactions to the substances tested.

Medical organizations have reviewed the method. A 1991 position statement from the Australian College of Allergy said Vega testing has no established scientific basis and no controlled trials supporting its usefulness.[2] A double-blind study cited by science commentator Steven Novella found that electrodermal testing could not distinguish atopic from non-atopic participants and that no operator did better than another.[1]

chain: Practitioner measures skin conductance while the patient holds substance vials
Readings are interpreted as sensitivities to foods or products
Dietary changes made in the hope of clearer, calmer skin
angle.text: Users seek electrodermal screening to find foods or products they believe affect their skin, then adjust their diet or routine accordingly. Researchers who have tested the method for allergy diagnosis report it did not distinguish allergic from non-allergic participants.

paras: In the typical description, the practitioner attaches electrodes to the patient and presses a metal probe to the skin while the patient holds vials containing substances, and a meter responds with varying values that the practitioner interprets.[1] Similar devices appear under names including Electroacupuncture according to Voll (EAV).[1][3]
Practitioners use the readings to suggest foods or substances that they say the patient is sensitive to, and to recommend dietary changes.[1]

A 2001 double-blind study that used skin prick testing as the reference standard concluded that electrodermal testing could not distinguish atopic from non-atopic participants, and that no operator performed better than any other. It concluded the method cannot be used to diagnose environmental allergies.[1]

The Australian College of Allergy stated in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1991 that no controlled trials supported Vega testing.[2] The American Cancer Society has concluded that evidence does not support use of EAV as a method that can diagnose, cure or otherwise help people with cancer.[3]

Steven Novella describes the Vegatest as pseudoscience that has the trappings of science without proper methodology. Stephen Barrett of Quackwatch, quoted by Novella, says the devices respond mainly to skin conductance, which is largely determined by how hard the probe is pressed.[1] Wikipedia classifies the broader electroacupuncture-according-to-Voll topic under pseudoscience and energy therapies.[3]
Practitioners regard the method as a screening aid for sensitivities. The Australian College of Allergy warned that Vega testing may lead to inappropriate treatment and expense.[2]

timeline.event: The Australian College of Allergy publishes a position statement on Vega testing in the Medical Journal of Australia.[2]
A double-blind study finds electrodermal testing could not distinguish atopic from non-atopic participants.[1]
